column2: SAF-MCP: Secure Agentic Framework for Model Context Protocol (formerly SAFE-MCP), Framework Model v2
column7: - Adversary behavior against agentic systems follows the same 14 objectives as MITRE ATT&CK, from resource development and initial access through exfiltration and impact. · - Attacker-controlled text, images, or audio that enter model context can make the model treat untrusted content as authoritative directions. · - Adversaries hide instructions in an MCP tool description or parameter schema to steer the model's tool selection and arguments against the user's intent. · - An MCP server can present a benign tool, gain approval, and later change that tool's metadata or code, so the host runs different behavior without new authorization. · - Attacker-influenced output from one tool can drive a later call to a distinct tool or server that uses authority the agent already holds. · - Content written into an agent's persistent memory can steer reasoning and tool decisions in a later session. · - Repeated, equivalent approval requests can wear a user down until one is accepted, which defeats the human gate on a tool call or data disclosure.
column8: - The check that gates a privileged tool call must run in host code or with a human that the model cannot reach, prompt, or speak for. · - Without a valid, unexpired, scope-matching authorization artifact, the host denies the privileged call; missing or malformed approvals never default to allow. · - The authorization artifact must name the specific tool, its arguments or their digest, the requesting session, and a short expiry. · - The right to request approval comes from the authenticated session role, never from text the model emitted or the user typed into the prompt. · - Any tool interaction, resource access, or capability grant that is not explicitly permitted is blocked by default. · - Privilege boundaries must be enforced at runtime during each tool execution as well as at configuration time, so revocations take effect immediately. · - A detection rule that passes synthetic fixtures counts as fixture_tested and must not be represented as production effectiveness.
column9: - Least privilege: the platform team grants each MCP tool the minimum privileges its function needs, so a compromised tool reaches only its granted scope. · - Privilege isolation: the host keeps tools at different privilege levels apart and blocks a lower-privilege tool from invoking a higher one without escalation controls. · - Control and data flow separation: the host takes control flow only from trusted queries and treats tool descriptions and API responses as data that cannot change execution. · - Tool integrity: tool developers sign tool descriptions, and the client verifies the signature before it loads any tool. · - Per-invocation capability brokering: a broker applies each tool's declared filesystem, network, and syscall manifest per call and issues a single-use token scoped to that call. · - Complete audit trail: the host logs every privilege decision, escalation, grant, denial, and timeout with request context so reviewers can reconstruct who approved what. · - Defense in depth: operators layer architectural, prevention, detection, and response controls, starting with SAF-M-1, SAF-M-2, SAF-M-6, and SAF-M-11 when resources are limited. · - Profile-scoped threat modeling: security teams select SAF Core plus the domain profiles that match their deployment, then map active techniques to their environment.

column2: Agent Privacy Risk Taxonomy V.01 (AILuminate Assessment Standard)
column7: - Traditional privacy models such as Solove's taxonomy and the NIST privacy risk model assume deterministic data flows, centralized storage, and clear perimeter boundaries. · - Agents act as dynamic data intermediaries that execute code, keep memory across sessions, and orchestrate external tools and protocols such as MCP. · - Agents favor task completion over data minimization, and MCP lacks field-level access controls that would limit the context shared with external tools. · - Attackers embed hidden payloads such as invisible text, metadata, or system commands in emails, websites, and documents that agents process at run time. · - Upstream agent components such as skill packages, tool descriptions, and MCP servers can be compromised to make an agent leak sensitive data during normal execution. · - A constant stream of runtime permission pop-ups leads users to approve risky actions without reading, which removes the protection of the consent gate. · - No standardized, scalable, privacy-preserving method exists for logging agent interactions across organizations, which slows root-cause analysis after an incident.
column8: - Intent-based inference of privacy preferences is probabilistic, so it cannot guarantee that an agent infers or follows a user's preferences in a provable way. · - Blocking an agent's access to one file or database does not stop it from reconstructing the restricted information through redundant or secondary sources. · - A manipulated agent with a code execution tool such as a Python REPL or bash shell can bypass LLM-level privacy controls and gain read and write access to the host. · - Regex and heuristic redaction pipelines fail to remove semantic PII and fuzzy quasi-identifiers, which can still re-identify users. · - Static, binary permission gates are structurally incompatible with the open-ended runtime reasoning of autonomous agents. · - A successful attack, agent action, or technical data exposure does not by itself show that downstream harm occurred.
column9: - Causal chain assessment: assessors trace each agent privacy risk from deployment condition or threat to failure mechanism, privacy event, affected party, privacy impact, and downstream harm. · - Evidence labeling: the assessor states which stages of the causal chain were directly observed and which remain inferred or uncertain. · - Bounded likelihood: assessors give likelihood as a probability only when observed data has a defined population, denominator, and period; otherwise they rate exposure and failure separately. · - Threat-conditioned failure evidence: assessors label each failure as seen in ordinary use, under a credible threat model with a defined attacker capability and budget, or plausible but unconfirmed. · - Affected-party impact: assessors rate impact by its effect on affected parties, weighing data sensitivity, recipients, persistence, and reversibility, beyond technical compromise alone.

column7: - Offensive cyber operations often target unpatched or misconfigured systems, overly broad permissions, and weak credentials; attackers rarely need a sophisticated exploit. · - Subverting an agent that guards a network could give an attacker broad, undetected access. · - An agent's effectiveness depends heavily on the tools it can access, the software around the model that runs tools and manages memory, and its integration into the operating environment. · - As AI-reported vulnerabilities increase, triage becomes the bottleneck, and OT environments at critical infrastructure operators often cannot be patched on demand. · - AI models can produce functionally correct code that still contains vulnerabilities such as unchecked memory allocation and missing input validation. · - False positives consume analyst time, erode trust in automated systems, and cause alert fatigue that leads teams to overlook genuine threats. · - Many existing cyber evaluations come from offensive security and measure success at discrete attack tasks, revealing little about defensive judgment.
column8: - Before agents receive greater autonomy, they must be hardened against prompt injection, data poisoning, and evasion attacks. · - A defensive agent introduces risks of its own because the agent itself becomes a high-value target for attackers. · - Finding a vulnerability is only a first step; organizations must be able to prioritize which ones to fix and develop deployable patches in a timely manner. · - Applying a patch requires confirming existing functionality still works, testing compatibility with current systems, and coordinating downtime, which can take weeks or months. · - Agentic code analysis and vulnerability discovery deliver far less value when strong authentication, timely patching, and vulnerability management are missing.
column9: - Fundamentals first: organizations put strong authentication, timely patching, and disciplined vulnerability management in place before they invest in autonomous agents. · - Staged deployment: security teams first automate alert triage, log analysis, and detection-rule drafting, then move to more transformative uses as confidence grows. · - Match autonomy to risk: the deploying organization sets each agent's autonomy by context and the consequence of error, granting more in lower-risk work such as code analysis. · - Zero trust: operators treat agents as untrusted components and constrain, log, and verify every agent action until agent security matures. · - Synchronous monitoring: a separate LLM reviews each proposed agent action before it executes, alongside chain-of-thought monitoring of the agent's reasoning traces. · - Human approval for consequential actions: escalation workflows route consequential agent decisions to a person, and agents work inside existing SOC tooling and playbooks. · - Evidence-backed detections: red and blue team agents run commands against test systems that mirror production and validate each proposed detection rule against real log data. · - Defensive evaluation under attack: evaluators test whether an agent makes sound decisions under uncertainty while adversaries are actively attacking.
